title: Pommes de terre sarladaises
subtitle: Duck fat-fried potatoes with garlic and parsley from the Périgord
excerpt: Sliced potatoes cooked slowly in duck fat with garlic and flat-leaf parsley. From Sarlat in the Dordogne, the traditional accompaniment to confit de canard and magret de canard.
sourceNotes: A regional dish from Sarlat-la-Canéda in the Périgord Noir. Widely documented in French regional cooking references including Curnonsky, La France Gastronomique (1921) and Raymond Sokolov, The Cook's Canon (2003). The Périgord's duck fat cooking tradition is well-established in the public domain.

content.text: Pommes de terre sarladaises are everything pommes boulangère is not: rich, gold, and deeply savoury from the duck fat they cook in. They come from Sarlat in the Périgord, the heartland of French duck and goose cookery, and they belong beside confit duck or a pan-seared duck breast. The garlic and parsley go in at the end, not the beginning, so they stay bright.

items.prepNote: waxy variety, peeled and sliced 3 mm thick
from a jar or reserved from confit

content.text: Rinse the sliced potatoes in cold water and dry thoroughly. Melt the duck fat in a large, wide, heavy frying pan over medium heat.

Add the potato slices to the pan in a single layer if possible, or in overlapping layers. Season well with salt and pepper. Cook over medium heat, turning the potatoes occasionally with a spatula, for 35 to 40 minutes until completely tender and golden on all sides. Do not rush this on high heat: slow cooking in the fat is what gives them their character.

When the potatoes are cooked through and golden, scatter over the garlic and parsley. Toss everything together and cook for 1 to 2 minutes until the garlic smells fragrant but has not coloured. Taste, adjust the seasoning, and serve immediately.

items.symptom: Potatoes are burning before they are cooked through
items.cause: Heat too high, or pan too dry
items.fix: Reduce to medium-low. Duck fat should coat the potatoes: add a little more if the pan looks dry.
Garlic always goes in at the end, with the parsley. 1 to 2 minutes over moderate heat is enough.

content.text: These potatoes are the signature side dish of the Périgord Noir and the Quercy. They are inseparable from confit de canard: the two often arrive on the same plate, the confit having been reheated in the same duck fat the potatoes cooked in. If you are cooking duck confit at home and have jar duck fat to hand, this is what you make alongside it. Goose fat works equally well and produces a very similar result.
